items.title: Characterizing the role of reasoning tokens in large language models as state over tokens
items.summary:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01303-y

When large language models ‘reason’ about a problem, they might still solve it differently from what their reasoning transcript suggest. In this Perspective, Levy et al. describe how one can start investigating the role of these reasoning tokens.
items.text:
Abstract
Large language models increasingly rely on generating reasoning tokens that appear to describe a reasoning process performed by the model to arrive at the answer. However, empirical evidence reveals that when read as text, these tokens are not a faithful explanation of the model’s actual reasoning process. To address this gap between appearance and function, we introduce the State over Tokens (SoT) conceptual framework. SoT reframes reasoning tokens not as a linguistic narrative, but as an externalized computational state—the mechanism that persists the computation across the separate generation cycles. The SoT framing explains how the tokens can drive correct reasoning without being a faithful explanation when read as text and surfaces previously overlooked research questions on these tokens. We discuss how it dispels two common misconceptions: that the text records the complete process, and that the model uses the words with the meanings a human reader ascribes to them. We argue that this framing offers a fruitful way to think about these tokens, one that captures their mechanics accurately while remaining simple and intuitive, and that adopting it opens research directions. To better understand the mechanism of large-language-model reasoning, research should move beyond reading the tokens as text and also focus on decoding them as state.
Similar content being viewed by others
Main
The assertion that large language models (LLMs) can reason now appears unremarkable1,2. A key factor in achieving this was training the models to generate a sequence of tokens before their final answer, which substantially improves performance3,4.
We refer to this sequence of symbols, which includes phrases such as ‘therefore’, ‘consider’ and ‘it follows that’, as the ‘reasoning tokens’, and explicitly distinguish this name from ‘reasoning text’, which is the same tokens when interpreted by a reader according to their English semantics. Treating the tokens as text is useful; if seen as derivations of the answer, they may help the reader verify individual steps and transitions between them, thus establishing trust in the answer5,6,7.
The combination of (1) utility in improving the answer, (2) appearance as an English text, and (3) utility of the text as a derivation of the answer often leads to interpreting the derivation in the text as reflective of the process done by the model when deriving the answer. This is strengthened by metaphors such as ‘chain-of-thought‘, which imply that the steps in the text are ‘thoughts’ that explain the process. However, there is a difference between a good derivation of the answer and an account of the process by which the model arrived at it—what we would call a faithful explanation. The reasoning text can provide the former, but falls short as the latter. Even the simple case of using the text to infer whether a hint planted in the input affected the output breaks down: the model can rely on the hint while omitting it from its reasoning text8,9 (see more in the ‘Plausibility without faithfulness’ section).
While those findings clarify what the reasoning tokens are not, they leave a conceptual vacuum as to what they are. Our aim in this Perspective is to help fill that vacuum. Drawing on the idea that metaphors structure understanding and guide thinking10, we believe that adopting more apt descriptions and metaphors can steer researchers and practitioners towards more fruitful directions and surface a new set of questions that are less salient under the prevailing view of the reasoning text as an explanation.
To understand reasoning tokens, the appearance of which can be deceiving (as empirical research has found), we propose a framing that captures their functional role accurately while remaining simple and intuitive. To this end, we advocate viewing them as representing a computational state embedded as tokens, what we consider State over Tokens (SoT). This view characterizes the reasoning tokens as a computational device that enables the persistence of a process across separate computation cycles. We portray the reasoning tokens as state carriers of a computational process, a frame that captures the mechanism accurately while remaining simple enough to be used productively in research and in everyday discourse.
The whiteboard analogy in Box 1 mirrors the model’s operation: the words are the reasoning tokens, you are the model and the 10-second interval represents the model’s limited capacity per cycle. Motivated by this intuition, we present the SoT framework (see ‘The State over Tokens framework’ section) and use it to demonstrate two common misconceptions that underlie the belief that the text is a faithful explanation (see ‘Two misconceptions behind the illusion of explanation’ section) and to examine its distinctive ontological divergence (see ‘The ontological divergence between text and state’ section).
The SoT framework naturally gives rise to new research questions (see ‘Questions raised by state over tokens’ section), challenging current interpretability methods to account for multiple cycles, and questioning whether language is a special computational medium that can theoretically act both as a state and as a faithful explanation.
Finally, this perspective compels us to reconsider established metaphors. While ‘chain-of-thought’ captures the sequential nature of generation, it misleadingly suggests that the text contains the complete reasoning process; SoT clarifies that tokens are the state passed between computations, and do not necessarily express the computations themselves. Similarly, the ‘scratchpad’ metaphor obscures a crucial distinction: while humans use a scratchpad to supplement internal memory, for LLMs, the tokens are what allows any persistence between cycles.
By establishing reasoning tokens as externalized computational state, the SoT framework characterizes how LLMs use what seems to us as natural language as a computational medium, and provides a foundation for future work on decoding how models use language tokens to reason.
The remainder of the Perspective is structured as follows. The ‘Reasoning tokens and reasoning text’ section introduces reasoning tokens as our object of study and reviews the empirical evidence that the reasoning text is not a faithful explanation of the model’s final answer. The ‘The State over Tokens framework’ section introduces the SoT framework formally. The ‘Two misconceptions behind the illusion of explanation’ section uses the framework to dispel two common misconceptions about the reasoning text. The ‘The ontological divergence between text and state’ section examines the divergence between the text and state interpretations of the same tokens. The ‘Questions raised by state over tokens’ section raises research questions opened by the framework.
Reasoning tokens and reasoning text
The subject of our discussion is the sequence of tokens that LLMs emit before their final answer, which we refer to as reasoning tokens (which we distinguish from reasoning text, which is the English interpretation of these same tokens). This approach started with prompting LLMs to generate reasoning tokens using examples or instructions such as ‘let’s think step by step’11,12,13 but now models are trained to generate those tokens regardless of the input3,4,14,15; in some cases, step-level verifiers that score the steps by their semantic content are used to improve the generation16,17,18. Those tokens are often separated from the final answer given to the user. The amount of reasoning is variable and consequential: generating more tokens before answering tends to improve accuracy19.
In this Perspective, we focus on characterizing the reasoning tokens. LLMs operate in the same way for the generation of the final answer as they do for the generation of reasoning tokens, but reasoning tokens differ from final-answer tokens in two specific ways that led us to focus our discussion on them.
The first reason is techno-sociological: reasoning tokens appear to offer a second product beyond the answer itself. When interpreted as English, the reasoning text reads like a description of reasoning work, encouraging readers to interpret them as not only what the model answers, but also how it seemingly arrived there, thereby providing a means of building trust20,21. This creates a conundrum specific to the reasoning tokens: the accuracy of the final answers keeps improving2, while at the same time, the empirical evidence that the reasoning text fails to reflect how those answers were produced (reviewed in the ‘Plausibility without faithfulness’ section) continues to mount.
The second reason is functional: we can conceptually distinguish the two stages by their training objectives. The final-answer tokens are generated to be interpreted by humans (or external systems) as the solution to the user’s query. During training, the answer text is optimized to reflect the solution, and thus has an additional constraint: its surface semantics must match human readers’ semantics. By contrast, the reasoning tokens are not constrained in this way, and their purpose is to support producing the final answer. Indeed, their existence improves the accuracy of the final answer3,15,19. This distinction is especially pronounced in models trained with methods that do not subject the reasoning tokens to specific constraints as long as they serve the final prediction4,22.
Plausibility without faithfulness
The reasoning text often reads like a logical derivation of the final answer. As Perrier7 notes, it can correspond to an explanation according to some deductive proof system, representing a sequence of steps that leads to a conclusion. However, while this may count as an explanation of the answer, it is not an explanation of the model, and in particular it does not explain the process by which the model reached the answer.
Explanations are central to building trust in artificial intelligence models20,21. By explanation, we mean a description, at some useful level of abstraction, of a process by which the input can be transformed into the given output, identifying which factors were responsible for this output rather than another and allowing the user to anticipate how the output would change under counterfactual inputs23,24. We take this causal, counterfactual-supporting notion of explanation as our working definition throughout the paper. An explanation can be plausible when it describes a process that could have led from the input to the output. An explanation is faithful when it reflects the process that led to the output, allowing the user to make accurate inferences about the model’s process and reliable predictions of its behaviour on counterfactual or related inputs.
When treated as natural-language text, the reasoning text might seem like a faithful explanation, but this appearance is deceiving. The tokens invite a human reading: applying the rules of natural-language semantics to interpret them at face value. Through this act of reading, the reasoning text can yield a plausible explanation: one that describes a process that would lead from the input to the answer7,25. However, it often does not yield a faithful explanation20: the account describes merely a process consistent with its answer, not the actual process that led from the input to the output. This failure of faithfulness manifests as incompleteness of the text and a semantic mismatch between the LLM and the reader.
Incompleteness
The reasoning text can be incomplete and omit critical factors that affected the model’s final answer8,9,26,27,28,29. A study conducted in controlled settings showed that LLMs can even seem to follow alignment goals while omitting the undesired topics from the reasoning text30.
Semantic mismatch between LLM and reader
The semantic content of the reasoning text can be meaningless or misleading from a human perspective. Some studies have found that LLMs can disregard specific details in the text they generate31,32,33. Other work has shown that LLMs can be trained to produce irrelevant reasoning text and still provide accurate final answers34,35,36. This also leads to the failure to identify causal relations in the generation process of the reasoning text37.
The peril lies in what we call the trust-calibration problem: the risk that plausibility can increase trust without justifying it, fostering over-reliance on model outputs. When reasoning text mimics systematic deliberation that includes certain factors that the users consider critical, this may lead them to place unwarranted trust in the model38,39.
What can be said on reasoning tokens
Following this growing body of evidence and the practical risks it highlights, some have already argued that we should not treat reasoning text as a faithful explanation of the model’s reasoning process40,41,42,43,44. However, we believe that we need to characterize the role of reasoning tokens in a positive way, beyond merely stating that they are not an explanation.
What can be said about the reasoning tokens? The following three statements hold.
- The reasoning tokens are an important part of the process that leads to the final answer.
- The reasoning tokens can sometimes be read as a series of steps that logically lead to the answer.
- The reasoning tokens are not a faithful explanation of the process that led to the final answer.
We would like a metaphor that accounts for all three of these points. In what follows, we provide the SoT view, which we believe does that.
The State over Tokens framework
Rather than explaining the reasoning tokens by how they are perceived by human readers (how they look), we consider their functional role within the mechanism of generation (what they do). We view reasoning tokens as an accumulated computational substrate—a medium through which the computation state is encoded in tokens.

items.title: Large language models discover complementary heuristics for combinatorial optimization
items.summary:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 01 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01307-8

Huatian Gong and colleagues developed LACE, a large language model-based framework that designs optimization algorithms. It builds a verified problem contract, then evolves a portfolio of complementary heuristics that together solve problems that no single method can handle.
items.text:
Abstract
Combinatorial optimization (CO) underpins decision-making across science, engineering and industry, especially manufacturing, logistics, healthcare operations and energy management. However, designing effective heuristics for each new problem variant requires deep domain knowledge and months of expert iteration. Directly prompting large language models (LLMs) can generate executable code, but single-pass synthesis of complete heuristics routinely fails on new CO problems. Here we introduce LLM-driven Algorithm Construction via Complementary Evolution (LACE), a framework that decomposes algorithm design into an input schema, output schema, tool library and heuristic portfolio (the \({\mathcal{I}}\)–\({\mathcal{O}}\)\({\mathcal{T}}\)\({\mathcal{H}}\) interface) and refines the portfolio through time-constrained complementary evolution. The interface specifies a verified problem contract under which the LLM operates, directing model capacity to high-level algorithmic reasoning rather than problem-specific implementation. Complementary evolution then iteratively generates and selects specialist heuristics capable of solving heterogeneous instances within strict runtime budgets. Across 36 classical CO-Bench problems, LACE attains an average score of 0.945, against 0.870 for the strongest existing LLM-based method and 0.571 for direct LLM prompting without any framework, locating the gain in the framework rather than the model. On four structurally new problems, LACE reaches 0.97–0.99, while five existing LLM-based baselines fail to produce any feasible algorithm. These results demonstrate that effective algorithm discovery for such problems can be automated to a substantial degree.
Similar content being viewed by others
Main
Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly expanded its scientific and technological reach, transforming domains from molecular biology1,2 and mathematical reasoning3,4 to reinforcement learning algorithm discovery5 and scientific prediction6. Yet these advances have not extended to automated algorithm design for combinatorial optimization (CO), in which discrete search spaces resist end-to-end learning or gradient-based approaches. This gap is consequential, as real-world systems in global logistics, manufacturing, healthcare operations and energy management rely on solving CO problems7,8,9,10. These problems typically exhibit exponentially growing search spaces, rendering exact solution methods computationally intractable11. This inherent complexity has driven the widespread adoption of heuristic algorithms, which provide approximate solutions within feasible timeframes12. However, deploying heuristics faces three compounding challenges: the structural diversity of CO problems precludes universal algorithms; effective heuristics must be manually crafted by domain experts through time-intensive iteration13; and the landscape of CO problems continuously expands through new variants and formulations14,15,16,17,18. These challenges create a pressing need for approaches that can automatically generate high-quality heuristics, without months of manual design effort per problem.
Large language models (LLMs) offer an intriguing opportunity in this direction17,19. Recent works demonstrate that LLMs can generate executable code20 and construct heuristics through iterative refinement and evolutionary search21,22,23,24,25. More recent agentic systems coordinate multiple LLM roles to translate a natural-language problem description into executable solvers26,27,28. However, existing LLM-based approaches exhibit a consistent structural limitation: most prompt LLMs to synthesize complete heuristics in a single pass4,21,22,29. Although effective for classical benchmarks with well-established patterns in pretraining corpora, this paradigm fails on structurally new CO problems, producing infeasible, non-executable or computationally intractable heuristics23,25. Two fundamental barriers underlie this limitation. First, synthesizing complete heuristics for unfamiliar constraint structures may exceed the compositional reasoning capacity of LLMs. Second, existing approaches do not guarantee that generated heuristics will meet practical runtime constraints during execution. These barriers raise two questions: (Q1) Generalization: What interface enables LLMs to generate heuristics that generalize robustly across structurally diverse CO problems, including problems unlikely to be well represented in their training corpora? (Q2) Efficiency: How can LLM-based heuristic generation systematically satisfy varying real-world runtime constraints, producing solutions that span the quality–time trade-off spectrum from emergency decisions to strategic planning?
We introduce LLM-driven Algorithm Construction via Complementary Evolution (LACE), a framework (Fig. 1) that addresses Q1 and Q2 through two synergistic mechanisms: universal modular decomposition and time-constrained complementary evolution. For generalization, LACE decomposes algorithm design into four modules—input schema \({\mathcal{I}}\), output schema \({\mathcal{O}}\), tool library \({\mathcal{T}}\) and heuristic portfolio \({\mathcal{H}}\)—providing a unified \({\mathcal{I}}\)–\({\mathcal{O}}\)–\({\mathcal{T}}\)–\({\mathcal{H}}\) interface for automated heuristic generation across diverse CO problems. The problem contract (\({\mathcal{I}}\), \({\mathcal{O}}\), \({\mathcal{T}}\)) is constructed automatically by an LLM agent from a natural-language problem statement, without per-problem human authoring; \({\mathcal{H}}\) is then generated by the LLM given this contract, focusing exclusively on algorithmic reasoning without mastering low-level implementation details for each new problem. For efficiency, LACE employs time-constrained complementary evolution to refine \({\mathcal{H}}\) through seven operators—five generation operators and two reactive repair operators—producing the complementary heuristic portfolios that give the method its name, by means of rank-aware selection that ensures each instance is covered by at least one specialist; by executing this process independently under multiple runtime budgets, LACE spans the quality–time trade-off from emergency decisions to strategic planning. We evaluate LACE on 40 CO problems spanning six families, consistently outperforming classical solvers and existing LLM-based approaches, and generalizing zero-shot to four structurally new problems where direct LLM synthesis fails entirely. These results demonstrate that automated heuristic discovery for new CO problems, traditionally a months-long expert effort, can be replaced by an automated procedure driven by a natural-language description alone.
Results
LACE overview
LACE operates through a two-stage architecture. Stage one employs universal modular decomposition to enable cross-problem generalization by decomposing algorithm design into four modules (\({\mathcal{I}}\)–\(\mathcal O\)–\(\mathcal T\)–\(\mathcal H\)), allowing LLMs to generate heuristics without constructing complete solvers for each problem. Stage two ensures computational efficiency through time-constrained complementary evolution, producing heuristic portfolios that span the quality–time trade-off spectrum and satisfy varying runtime constraints.
Stage one: universal modular decomposition
To achieve generalization across structurally diverse CO problems, LACE decomposes algorithm design into four modules: an input designer, which defines the input schema \({\mathcal{I}}\) describing problem input data; an output designer, which defines the output schema \({\mathcal{O}}\) describing the required solution output structure; a tool designer, which encapsulates complex domain logic into a callable tool library \({\mathcal{T}}=\{{\tau }_{1},\ldots ,{\tau }_{K}\}\) containing a feasibility checker, an objective evaluator and problem-specific helpers; and a heuristic generator, which produces an initial portfolio \({{\mathcal{H}}}_{0}\) in which each heuristic is a self-contained solve function \(h:{\mathcal{I}}\to {\mathcal{O}}\) taking an input from \({\mathcal{I}}\) and returning a feasible output in \({\mathcal{O}}\). Each heuristic invokes tools from \({\mathcal{T}}\) to internally construct a feasible solution. Crucially, this separation of the problem contract (encoded in \({\mathcal{I}}\), \({\mathcal{O}}\), \({\mathcal{T}}\)) from algorithmic reasoning (encoded in \({\mathcal{H}}\)) enables LLMs to focus on high-level decision-making without mastering low-level implementation details for each new problem (see Methods for full specifications).
Stage two: time-constrained complementary evolution
Stage two refines \({{\mathcal{H}}}_{0}\) into a final complementary portfolio \({{\mathcal{H}}}^{* }\) explicitly optimized for heterogeneous instances under strict runtime constraints Tmax. The evolution process iteratively applies five generation operators—local refinement (LR), reflective redesign (RR), complementary crossover (CC), comparative synthesis (CS) and diversity injection (DI)—to generate candidate heuristics that target distinct limitations of the current portfolio. These are complemented by two reactive repair operators—error repair (ER) and efficiency improvement (EI)—which are triggered automatically when candidates fail execution or exceed the runtime budget. Generated candidates combine with the current portfolio to form a pool of 2n heuristics, from which n are retained by way of a ranking-based complementary selection objective that minimizes the average best rank across all instances, ensuring balanced coverage regardless of instance scale. To accommodate diverse operational requirements, stage two is executed independently under multiple time budget settings, producing portfolios that span the quality–time trade-off spectrum from emergency decisions to strategic planning (see Methods for operator definitions and selection formulation).
Performance on classical benchmarks
We evaluate LACE on CO-Bench30, a third-party benchmark of 36 CO problems, which we group into five problem families: scheduling; routing and graphs; packing and cutting; location and assignment; and selection and knapsack. Methods are scored under CO-Bench’s protocol on three metrics—Avg Score (a primal-gap-style normalized quality score), Valid Rate (the fraction of problems on which the generated heuristic algorithm yields feasible solutions on every test instance) and Survival Rate (the fraction of test instances reaching at least 99% of the best-known objective)—with all LLM-based methods sharing OpenAI o3 Mini as the backbone for fair comparison.
LACE leads on all three metrics (Fig. 2a). Valid Rate score for LACE reaches 0.944, whereas no other LLM-based baselines exceed 0.611. This means that these methods produce infeasible solutions on at least one test instance for nearly 40% of CO-Bench problems, whereas LACE delivers heuristic algorithms with full feasibility on essentially every problem. Avg Score for LACE reaches 0.945, exceeding the strongest LLM-based baseline (0.870) and the classical solver suite (0.797); the bare-LLM baseline, in which OpenAI o3 Mini is prompted to produce a heuristic algorithm directly without any framework, achieves only 0.571, demonstrating that the gains stem from the \({\mathcal{I}}\)\({\mathcal{O}}\)\({\mathcal{T}}\)\({\mathcal{H}}\) decomposition and complementary evolution rather than the LLM backbone alone. Survival Rate for LACE reaches 0.623, more than 17 percentage points above any previous baseline, indicating that the majority of test instances are solved to near-optimality. The advantage holds within every family (Fig. 2b): LACE attains the highest Avg Score in all five. The same modular interface, generated automatically from each problem’s natural-language description without per-problem authoring, supports heuristic discovery across structurally diverse CO problems.
Zero-shot generalization to new problems
A stronger test of generalization is whether LACE can synthesize effective heuristics for problems that are, to the best of our knowledge, newly formulated and therefore unlikely to be well represented in LLM training corpora. We design four such problems centred on container-terminal logistics: a port scheduling problem (PSP) and three tugboat-routing variants (TRS, MB-TRS and TRS-VS) introducing multi-depot dispatch and speed-dependent fuel coupling.
Across the four problems (Fig. 3a–d), LACE attains Avg Scores of 0.981, 0.990, 0.978 and 0.969. Gurobi reaches 0.53 within 1 min and 0.64 within 30 min, as its integer formulations do not converge to global optima at the tested sizes. Six tuned metaheuristics range from 0.72 to 0.96 on the first three problems and degrade to 0.54–0.58 on TRS-VS, where the increased problem complexity leads to substantially worse performance. Under the same OpenAI o3 Mini backbone, five LLM-based methods (FunSearch, EoH, EoH-S, Greedy Refine and ReEvo) produce no feasible algorithm on any of the four problems; HeurAgenix returns feasible but substantially weaker solutions than LACE (0.23–0.58). These results demonstrate that LACE’s modular decomposition enables zero-shot generalization to structurally new problems, a capability that existing LLM-based methods fail to achieve.
Contributions of tool library and portfolio
LACE derives its effectiveness from two structural mechanisms: the tool library \({\mathcal{T}}=\{{\tau }_{1},{\tau }_{2},\ldots ,{\tau }_{K}\}\), which provides the LLM with reusable building blocks for heuristic construction, and the heuristic portfolio of size n, which combines specialized algorithms across the instance space. We quantify the contribution of each.

items.title: Regional climate risk assessment from climate models using probabilistic machine learning
items.summary:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 28 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01308-7

A generative AI framework called GenFocal is introduced for climate downscaling, producing realistic fine-scale weather from coarse projections and improving regional risk estimates of compound extremes such as heatwaves and tropical cyclones.

Abstract
Effective climate risk assessment is hindered by the resolution gap between coarse global climate models and the fine-scale information needed for regional decision making. Existing downscaling methods struggle to bridge this gap: physics-based methods are too computationally expensive for large ensemble sampling of extreme events, while traditional statistical methods fail to capture multivariate spatiotemporal dependencies crucial to compound risk estimation. Furthermore, current machine learning approaches rely on temporally aligned training pairs, which are unavailable for free-running climate projections. Here we introduce GenFocal, an AI framework that generates statistically accurate, fine-scale weather from coarse climate projections without requiring paired simulated and observed events during training. GenFocal synthesizes complex and long-lived hazards, such as heatwaves and tropical cyclones, even when they are not well represented in the coarse climate projections. It also samples high-impact, rare events more accurately than leading methods. By translating large-scale climate projections into actionable localized information, GenFocal provides a powerful paradigm to improve climate adaptation and resilience strategies.

Main
Effective economic and societal planning over horizons from years to decades is increasingly hinging on understanding and predicting how climate changes. While global climate models (GCMs) provide robust projections of large-scale trends, their coarse resolution creates a critical information gap for local and regional decision-making1. This gap limits risk assessments for infrastructure design2, energy system planning3, flood forecasting4 and financial services such as insurance pricing5. The challenge is particularly acute when assessing compound events, such as concurrent heat and drought, where complex spatiotemporal correlations are not resolved by GCMs, yet drive the most severe effects6,7,8. Bridging this scale gap is a grand computational and scientific challenge, and the primary obstacle to translating climate science into actionable intelligence for climate adaptation and resilience strategies.
This global-to-regional translation is fundamentally a problem of characterizing the statistics of fine-scale physical processes from coarse-grained climate projections. The large computational cost of GCMs restricts them to coarse grids, which inherently limits their fidelity and introduces biases. Furthermore, the chaotic nature of the climate system means that directly aligning coarse climate simulations with local weather observations at fine temporal scales is impossible. Historically, this lack of alignment has seriously hampered the development of a general statistical mapping from GCM outputs to consistent local weather that reliably preserves the complex correlation structures needed for accurate regional climate risk assessment. In particular, this consistency with local weather is essential to near-term climate risk assessment where the statistical characterization must be grounded in past observations8.
Existing efforts to overcome this downscaling challenge aim to correct biases and add coherent, fine-scale detail to coarse GCM outputs. Physics-based dynamical downscaling uses regional climate models forced by GCMs to simulate climate processes at higher resolution. They capture the rich spatiotemporal correlations of climate processes, but their computational expense limits the uncertainty quantification and robust assessment of extreme events, which requires a large number of samples9,10. Statistical downscaling methods are a computationally efficient alternative, but they often lack the flexibility to capture the full range of spatiotemporal correlations that define complex weather and compound events11. Recent advances in machine learning have spurred a new generation of machine learning-based downscaling methods that have shown great promise in weather forecasting and regional climate model emulation12,13,14. However, these methods predominantly rely on a supervised learning paradigm that requires temporally aligned pairs of low-resolution and high-resolution data for training. This requirement poses a substantial challenge for downscaling climate projections, for which corresponding high-resolution ground truth data are unavailable.
We propose GenFocal, a computationally efficient, general-purpose generative artificial intelligence (AI) framework that addresses this grand challenge. GenFocal rapidly generates large ensembles of weather realizations that are physically realistic and statistically consistent with conditioning coarse climate projections. It is capable of elucidating complex, fine-scale weather phenomena from coarse climate data sources where those phenomena are poorly resolved.
GenFocal yields higher-fidelity local climate information than well-established statistical methods, including those used in leading reports such as the US Fifth National Climate Assessment. By modelling spatial and temporal correlations, GenFocal can capture the risk and evolution of spatiotemporal extremes—such as heatwaves and tropical cyclones (TCs)—in a unified framework: a capability that is well beyond current statistical models.
GenFocal
Figure 1 provides a schematic of the algorithmic pipeline for GenFocal, highlighting its key innovations (see Supplementary Information, section 9 for complete details). GenFocal incorporates three main features, namely two distinct generative AI techniques for bias correction and super-resolution, alongside the explicit modelling of temporal sequences of consecutive weather states at both the coarse-scale and fine-scale levels. Together, these features make GenFocal capable of probabilistically mapping coarse climate projections to fine-grained weather fields with strong temporal coherence, enabling the accurate characterization of complex, multi-day events such as prolonged heatwaves or TCs.
In this work, GenFocal downscales coarse climate states (\({\mathcal{Y}}\) in Fig. 1) from \(1.{5}^{\circ}\) resolution to fine-grained weather states (\({\mathcal{X}}\) in Fig. 1) at \(0.2{5}^{\circ}\) resolution in a localized region, using an intermediate latent space (\({\mathcal{Y}}{\prime}\) in Fig. 1) of coarse-grained weather states matching the resolution of \({\mathcal{Y}}\). The input features 10 daily averaged variables, while the output contains 4 variables sampled 2-hourly (Supplementary Table 5). GenFocal is trained on 20 years (1980–1999) of data, using the publicly available ERA5 reanalysis15 as the high-resolution target and the Community Earth System Model Version 2 (CESM2) Large Ensemble (LENS2)16 as the coarse-resolution source. Hyperparameter tuning was performed using the period 2000–2009, and the final evaluation is reported for the 10-year period 2010–2019, downscaling the full LENS2 ensemble. This chronological split for training, validation and testing aligns with the intended application of assessing climate risk over the next few decades8. Details can be found in Supplementary Information, section 6 (including the data used) and Supplementary Information, section 9 (including details on the frameworks, neural architectures, training and hyperparameter tuning).
Catalysed by the recent emergence of generative AI models, a few recent studies have explored generative modelling in weather forecasting17,18 and downscaling12. We provide a detailed review of these modern machine learning techniques, alongside traditional methods, in Supplementary Information, section 1. A key limitation of existing approaches is their reliance on temporally aligned source and target data, generally unavailable when bridging coarse climate simulations with historical weather records. GenFocal is designed to overcome the scientific challenge of correlational modelling of chaotic systems by operating without this alignment assumption. It offers the scalability needed for real-world datasets and has undergone thorough methodological verification.
Realistic genesis and evolution of TCs
TCs are exceptionally destructive natural hazards responsible for thousands of deaths and tens of billions of dollars in damages every year. The success of mitigation strategies depends heavily on reliable projections of TC frequency, intensity and tracks under different climate scenarios. High-fidelity simulation of fine-grained physical processes is necessary for driving TC genesis and evolution, requiring much higher resolutions than those afforded by current GCMs. Physics-based dynamical downscaling via regional climate models can accurately capture the evolution of individual TCs, but it remains too expensive to generate the vast amount of data necessary to assess regional TC risk19. Studying future TC risk with statistical downscaling is possible, but only through bespoke methods that do not capture their interaction with the environment, and emulate TCs with reduced order systems that are partially coherent with their underlying physics20.
By contrast, GenFocal is able to capture the full life cycle of TCs, from genesis to maturity (Supplementary Fig. 2), without specifically targeting these emergent extreme phenomena in our model design and training. As shown in Fig. 2 for the North Atlantic basin, GenFocal is able to generate TCs on the basis of the input’s large-scale conditions, even when these storms are largely absent from the input climate projections (Methods and Supplementary Information, section 8). This ability crucially broadens GenFocal’s applicability compared to methods reliant on input data at resolutions beyond those routinely available from climate models13,20.
GenFocal generates TCs with tracks (Fig. 2d,g), cyclogenesis locations (Fig. 2b), landfalls (Fig. 2c), frequency (Fig. 2h), intensity (Fig. 2f,i) and morphology (Fig. 2e and Supplementary Fig. 9) consistent with the ERA5 reanalysis and the target resolution21 over the test period 2010–2019. This is in stark contrast with the statistics and tracks identified in the coarse LENS2, which exhibit both a lower frequency and excessively long durations (Fig. 2a,e).
Accurate assessment of compound climate risk
The risk of compound extremes arises from the cumulative effect of interacting physical processes, such as wildfires fuelled by dry vegetation and fanned by strong winds. This type of interdependency is often underestimated by downscaling methods that neglect correlations between hazards and their timescales6,22. Humid heatwaves, characterized by prolonged periods of high temperature and humidity, are among the most frequent and impactful of such events, straining human health and power grids. We evaluate the ability of GenFocal to represent humid heatwaves by analysing the risk of summer heat index extremes in the Conterminous United States (CONUS) across timescales (Fig. 3). The physical and spatial structure of heatwaves is further examined in terms of the tail dependence of temperature and humidity extremes and the spatial autocorrelation, respectively. (For the definitions of these metrics, see Supplementary Information, section 7.)
GenFocal yields accurate estimates of the 99th percentile of the heat index during the summer months, with an average bias reduction over 35% with respect to the statistical downscaling baselines, which systematically underestimate risk (Fig. 3f,k,p). Furthermore, the tail dependence of temperature and humidity extremes demonstrates its superior ability to capture concurrent hazards, with notable improvements across the midwest and the western USA (Fig. 3g,l,q). These improvements amount to an average error reduction of 44% with respect to Seasonal Trends and Analysis of Residuals Empirical-Statistical Downscaling Model (STAR-ESDM) and Bias Correction and Spatial Disaggregation (BCSD). GenFocal also reproduces the spatial structure of weather patterns, which is strongly affected by fine-scale processes characteristic of regions with diverse topography such as California. The spatial correlations of the heat index and wind speed over this region with respect to San Francisco are shown in Fig. 3d,e, evaluated from the ERA5 reanalysis data. GenFocal captures the summertime decorrelation in the heat index between San Francisco and inland California driven by the coastal cooling effect of sea breeze, which increases with inland temperatures23 (Fig. 3i). GenFocal also reproduces the complex spatial correlations of wind speed modulated by changes in topography (Fig. 3j). Downscaling methods that do not model spatial correlations explicitly, such as BCSD and STAR-ESDM, typically fail to identify the rich spatial correlation structure from the coarse climate simulation (Fig. 3n,o,s,t).
Heat-related mortality increases with heatwave duration24, highlighting the importance of estimating the risk of extended periods of extreme heat. Capturing persistent events requires adequate representation of the temporal coherence of climate fields, which GenFocal models explicitly. We assess the skill at predicting extended heatwaves by estimating the risk of 5-day streaks with daily maximum heat indices exceeding 305 K. This threshold corresponds to the ‘extreme caution’ heat advisory of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. GenFocal provides largely unbiased estimates of 5-day extreme caution heat streaks across the east coast and the midwest, compared with the statistical downscaling methods, which tend to overestimate risk in these regions (Fig. 3h,m,r). Overall, GenFocal reduces average bias by 44% and 57% compared to BCSD and STAR-ESDM, respectively.

items.title: Towards foundation-style models for energy-frontier heterogeneous neutrino detectors via self-supervised pretraining
items.summary:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01309-6

Alonso-Monsalve et al. demonstrate that self-supervised pretraining helps deep learning models to interpret complex neutrino detector events, improving classification, reconstruction and data efficiency while enabling transfer across different neutrino detector technologies.
items.text:
Abstract
Accelerator-based neutrino physics is entering an energy-frontier regime in which interactions reach the tera-electronvolt scale and produce exceptionally dense, overlapping detector signatures. Event interpretation is impractical for conventional reconstruction and challenging for supervised models trained from scratch, particularly when labelled data are scarce and analyses span diverse objectives. Here we present a sparse Vision Transformer framework for learning reusable representations from heterogeneous detector data. Self-supervised pretraining combines masked-autoencoder reconstruction with relational voxel-level objectives for hierarchy, ghost and particle identification, followed by joint fine-tuning across classification and regression tasks. On simulated events from the proposed FASER calorimeter (FASERCAL) concept, pretraining improves neutrino-flavour and charm-quark identification, momentum regression and vertex reconstruction, with relational objectives providing further gains in topologically complex channels. Attribution and representation diagnostics show a more structured latent space, while detector-subsystem ablations recover physically plausible channel-dependent roles. With roughly 103 labelled events, the pretrained encoder matches the flavour-classification performance of scratch training with an order of magnitude more data. Cross-domain transfer is observed on public plastic-scintillator and liquid-argon benchmarks. A matched alternative-generator stress test shows stable flavour and kinematic performance while exposing charm tagging as generator sensitive. These results support self-supervised multimodal pretraining as a route towards reusable detector representations. We use ‘foundation-style’ in this restricted sense, rather than claiming a completed general-purpose detector foundation model.

Main
Accelerator-based neutrino physics is entering the energy frontier. Forward collider-neutrino programmes extend measurements into the tera-electronvolt regime, enabling neutrino-interaction studies and cross-section measurements at previously unexplored energies while broadening the case for collider neutrinos as a high-energy physics programme1,2,3,4,5,6. Yet, the same regime produces detector data of exceptional complexity. Interaction topologies become highly collimated, particle multiplicities rise, electromagnetic and hadronic activity overlap strongly and information must be integrated across heterogeneous detector systems. Machine learning is already widely used across particle physics for detector inference, anomaly detection or event reconstruction, and that broader landscape has been reviewed extensively7,8,9,10,11,12. In energy-frontier neutrino detection, however, the challenge is not simply whether learned models outperform existing pipelines but whether any practical analysis of these events is feasible without them.
Within accelerator neutrino experiments, convolutional, graph-based and transformer-like models have been shown to improve event classification, semantic segmentation or clustering on simulated detector data13,14,15,16,17,18,19,20,21. Most of literature, however, concerns lower-energy environments, individual detector subsystems or task-specific supervised models trained from scratch, often in settings where conventional reconstruction remains plausible. The regime considered here is qualitatively different: event topologies are so dense, collimated and overlapping that the challenge is not to refine an existing analysis chain but to construct a viable one.
The FASER calorimeter (FASERCAL) concept, a proposed upgrade for the FASER experiment at CERN, provides a stringent case study for this problem22. Its highly granular three-dimensional (3D) calorimeter (3DCAL) comprises over 460,000 readout voxels, only a fraction of which are active in a given event, and is followed by electromagnetic (ECAL) and hadronic (AHCAL) calorimeters and a muon spectrometer. The forward neutrino beam contains νe, νμ and ντ components, and the analyses considered here target both charged-current (CC) and neutral-current (NC) interactions. A model must therefore integrate sparse 3D volumetric inputs with heterogeneous auxiliary streams of different dimensionality. The resulting events, shown in Fig. 1, contain dense shower cores, extended secondary tracks, partial containment and deeply ambiguous local configurations. In this setting, machine learning-based analysis is not an optional enhancement to an otherwise tractable reconstruction problem; it is a mandatory prerequisite for practical event-level physics extraction.
This is precisely the setting in which representation learning becomes compelling. High-fidelity simulation provides abundant detector responses, but labelled targets remain task specific and expensive to produce. Masked modelling has emerged as a strong route to transferable representations in language, vision and structured data23,24,25,26,27,28. In neutrino and particle physics, recent studies have begun exploring transfer learning, domain adaptation, contrastive learning and masked point modelling29,30,31,32,33,34,35,36. What remains missing is a unified approach for learning reusable models for genuinely heterogeneous detectors in the extreme topological regime of energy-frontier neutrino interactions.
Our aim is to take a concrete step towards foundation-style models for neutrino detector data. We do not claim a completed general-purpose model; instead, we target the core ingredients such a model requires: broad self-supervised pretraining; reused across several downstream tasks; strong performance when only a few hundred to a few thousand labelled events are available; and transfer across detector technologies and energy scales. In this manuscript, ‘foundation-style’ therefore has an operational meaning: a single reusable encoder is trained with objectives independent of downstream task labels on a large detector sample, adapted to several supervised physics tasks, tested under limited-label conditions, probed with a matched alternative-generator sample and reused outside the source detector. A full detector foundation model would require broader detector coverage, stronger systematic validation and ultimately experimental-data calibration. We address this with a sparse vision-transformer (ViT)-like37 framework that combines masked-autoencoder (MAE)24 pretraining with relational voxel-level objectives available from simulation. The encoder is later fine-tuned on flavour identification, charmed-quark identification, event kinematics and vertex reconstruction; stress-tested on matched GENIE and NuWro samples; and evaluated for transfer on public datasets outside the source domain.
This paper makes three main contributions.
- 
                (1)
                
                  We introduce a sparse encoder for heterogeneous detector data that combines sparse convolutional patch embeddings, module-aware self-attention and Perceiver-IO fusion across calorimetric and tracking streams.
- 
                (2)
                
                  We formulate a multimodal pretraining strategy that augments masked reconstruction with relational voxel-level targets (ghost identification, interaction hierarchy and particle category), and show in the in-domain comparisons that include all three baselines that this composite objective improves downstream performance beyond MAE-only pretraining, with the largest gains in the most challenging channels.
- 
                (3)
                
                  We demonstrate that the learned representation improves performance and data efficiency across a multi-task fine-tuning suite and transfers beyond the source domain to publicly available benchmarks spanning different detector technologies and energy regimes. We also include a matched GENIE-to-NuWro evaluation of the final MAE + Rel to probe generator dependence without retraining and report the cross-domain transfer summaries for all three initialization strategies.
We evaluate this framework first on simulated events from the FASERCAL concept as an energy-frontier case study, including a matched GENIE-to-NuWro stress test, and then on public transfer benchmarks covering a variety of detector technologies and energy scales. The ‘Results’ therefore moves from pretraining behaviour to downstream classification, regression, attribution and representation diagnostics; data efficiency; and a combined robustness-and-transfer evaluation. The ‘Discussion’ interprets what these findings imply for representation learning in detector physics and the Methods describe the case-study data, architecture, training strategy and transfer setup.
Results
All downstream comparisons use the same architecture under three initialization strategies:
- 
                1.
                
                  Scratch: the fine-tuning architecture with standard random initialization of all trainable parameters.
- 
                2.
                
                  MAE: the same downstream architecture and randomly initialized task heads, with the encoder initialized from masked-reconstruction pretraining.
- 
                3.
                
                  MAE + Rel: the same downstream architecture and randomly initialized task heads, with the encoder initialized from the full pretraining objective that combines masked reconstruction with voxel-level relational tasks.
Throughout the downstream results, Scratch, MAE and MAE + Rel denote the fully fine-tuned multi-task models, not frozen encoders.
Pretraining
The pretraining tasks are intended to shape the latent representation rather than to serve as end products, so we present them primarily as qualitative evidence. Figure 1 shows masked-reconstruction examples on test events. Even with 75% of occupied patches masked, the model recovers broad shower envelopes, elongated track-like structures and coherent energy flow into missing regions. The reconstructions are not exact, particularly in dense shower cores and around fine secondary structures, and we do not interpret them as precise generative predictions. Their value is diagnostic: the encoder is forced to infer non-local spatial correlations rather than copying visible voxels. The relational objectives are also shown in Fig. 1. The model predicts ghost labels, hierarchy labels and particle-category labels on kept patches, again on test events. Here, ghost voxels are reconstructed deposits with no matched true particle, hierarchy labels distinguish background, primary and secondary activity, and particle-category labels separate electromagnetic, muonic and hadronic deposits. These targets are especially demanding: a single reconstructed voxel can receive contributions from multiple true particles, yielding soft class mixtures rather than hard one-hot assignments. Agreement with ground truth is the strongest in well-separated tracks and along the dominant shower axes, while the densest overlapping regions remain the most difficult. This is consistent with the detector challenge described in ref. 22: dense occupancy and view ambiguities create ghost activity and complicate local pattern assignment. Taken together, the reconstruction and relational results in Fig. 1 suggest that the encoder captures meaningful spatial and semantic correlations before any downstream fine-tuning is applied.
Classification and regression
The downstream classification and regression results are shown together in Fig. 2. The figure combines the most diagnostic classification panels with an all-class regression summary, while the operating-point scans and class-resolved regression box plots are shown in Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2. Performance is evaluated with one-versus-rest receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, row-normalized confusion matrices and the figure of merit \({{\rm{FOM}}}=S/\sqrt{S+B}\), where S and B denote the expected signal and background yields after thresholding. For flavour classification, CC ντ events are split into τ → e, τ → μ and τ → had according to whether an electron or muon appears among the primary tau-decay products; all remaining CC ντ events are assigned to the hadronic class. For charm classification, events are assigned to charm → μ if any primary charm-decay product is a muon, to charm → e otherwise if any primary charm-decay product is an electron and to charm → had for the remaining charm decays. The overall pattern is clear. MAE already improves the dominant channels, while MAE + Rel provides the largest gains for the less abundant and more topologically complex signatures.
For the dominant channels, the gains are consistent. The νe CC area under the ROC curve increases from 0.968 for Scratch to 0.983 for MAE and 0.985 for MAE + Rel, the νμ CC area under the curve (AUC) increases from 0.909 to 0.955 and 0.958, and the NC AUC increases from 0.885 to 0.943 and 0.947. The row-normalized confusion matrices also become more diagonal for the common categories. For example, the νe CC diagonal entry rises from 0.71 to 0.84 and 0.85, while the NC diagonal rises from 0.50 to 0.71 and 0.70. This suggests that masked reconstruction effectively captures the global event morphology needed for the dominant classes.
The most consequential gains appear in the tau-neutrino channels. The threshold scans supporting the quoted maximum figure of merit values are shown in Supplementary Fig. 1. items.text:
Biomedical discovery has entered an era in which the limiting resource is no longer data, but our ability to integrate and interpret evidence. DeepEvidence, a new deep research agent, goes beyond retrieving facts and constructs explicit representations of scientific evidence.
Subjects
The scientific literature now grows by millions of publications each year, while biological knowledge is distributed across hundreds of specialized databases, ontologies and knowledge graphs. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have dramatically improved information retrieval and question answering; however, transforming fragmented evidence into coherent biological understanding remains fundamentally challenging. In a recent study in Nature Machine Intelligence, Wang et al.1 present DeepEvidence, an artificial intelligence (AI) system that shifts the emphasis from retrieving biomedical information towards conducting structured scientific investigation through systematic evidence exploration and synthesis. Instead of simply answering questions, the system attempts to build an explicit representation of scientific evidence as it reasons.
The emergence of LLMs has rapidly changed expectations of what AI can contribute to scientific research2,3. Early applications largely focused on summarization, literature mining or retrieval-augmented question answering. More recently, the field has moved towards agentic systems capable of planning, tool use and autonomous execution of research workflows. Systems such as Biomni4, ToolUniverse5 and OpenAI’s Deep Research6 have demonstrated that language models can coordinate searches, invoke specialized tools and synthesize information across several resources. At the same time, broader efforts such as AI Co-Scientist7, autonomous chemistry platforms3 and Virtual Lab8 have begun to explore how AI might participate in scientific discovery more directly.
Yet despite these advances, a persistent limitation remains. Most existing systems remain fundamentally answer- rather than process-centric. As a result, they perform shallow searches to retrieve relevant documents and invoke tools from a large search space, and do not acknowledge structural relationships within their evidence. This can naturally lead to issues with relevancy, coherence and specificity. Human scientific reasoning follows a different approach. Scientists rarely arrive at conclusions based on a handful of papers, particularly for non-trivial questions. They iteratively accumulate evidence, choose tools purposefully rather than exhaustively, reconcile conflicting observations, and gradually construct an internal mental model that evolves as new information becomes available. Scientific discovery is therefore less about finding individual facts than about organizing evidence into coherent explanatory frameworks.
DeepEvidence is notable because it explicitly attempts to model this process. Instead of treating literature retrieval as the end point of reasoning, Wang et al. propose a framework in which several specialized agents ‘collaborate’ to explore heterogeneous biomedical knowledge sources using complementary search strategies1. Breadth-first exploration rapidly surveys multiple knowledge resources to identify potentially relevant entities, whereas depth-first exploration recursively follows mechanistic and citation links to investigate promising directions in greater detail. Throughout this process, the system continuously constructs an evidence graph that records entities, relationships, observations and provenance, providing a structured memory of the investigation rather than relying entirely on the language model’s internal context window. It shows that informed, staged search beats undirected exploration in large heterogeneous knowledge bases. DeepEvidence’s plan–act–observe–replan loop is a direct attempt to mirror the scientific reasoning process. It maintains an explicit, revisable checklist that gets updated as each subagent reports its findings, rather than committing to an answer after a single retrieval pass (Fig. 1).
Although evidence graphs and knowledge graphs are well established within biomedical informatics, their role in the work by Wang et al.1 is different. Namely, the evidence graph functions as an evolving external representation of the research process itself. This distinction is subtle but important. Existing graph-based systems generally assume that knowledge has already been organized into a unified graph before reasoning begins. However, biomedical knowledge is fragmented across publications, pathway databases, protein annotations, disease ontologies, clinical trial repositories and numerous specialized resources that differ in structure, completeness and terminology. DeepEvidence attempts to construct a coherent evidence representation dynamically as the investigation proceeds.
The implications extend beyond biomedical literature search. The authors demonstrate applications across several stages of translational research, including target identification, mechanistic pathway reasoning, metabolic response prediction, clinical trial design and evidence-based medicine. These tasks share a common requirement: integrating heterogeneous evidence while maintaining mechanistic consistency and traceable provenance. The work suggests that successful biomedical AI systems may increasingly depend on how they organize and reason over evidence rather than simply on the size of the underlying language model.
This observation aligns with a broader shift occurring across scientific AI. The first generation of scientific foundation models demonstrated remarkable predictive capabilities, exemplified by AlphaFold9 and later AlphaMissense10, which transformed protein structure prediction and variant interpretation through specialized machine learning. More recent systems have focused on scientific reasoning itself. AI Co-Scientist7 explores collaborative hypothesis generation, Biomni4 provides general-purpose biomedical tool use, while Virtual Lab8 demonstrates autonomous iterative experimentation. DeepEvidence occupies an interesting position within this landscape. Rather than competing directly on predictive modelling or laboratory automation, it focuses on a different bottleneck: evidence synthesis. In doing so, it highlights that scientific reasoning may require capabilities distinct from both prediction and retrieval.
At the same time, important challenges remain before evidence-centric AI systems become routine components of biomedical research. One concerns the distinction between provenance and correctness. Recording where information originates does not necessarily guarantee that conclusions are valid. Biomedical literature is characterized by publication bias, conflicting experimental findings, varying methodological quality and context-dependent biological effects. DeepEvidence records these observations with explicit provenance, but ultimately relies on the underlying language model to reconcile contradictory evidence. Future systems may need explicit probabilistic reasoning, uncertainty quantification and evidence-weighting frameworks that distinguish high-confidence causal relationships from preliminary or conflicting observations.
A second challenge concerns evaluation itself. The benchmarks presented by Wang et al.1 are comprehensive and span many stages of biomedical discovery. Nevertheless, benchmark performance is unlikely to become the ultimate measure of scientific AI. The success of biomedical reasoning systems should arguably be evaluated by their ability to generate useful scientific discoveries, prioritize experimentally validated hypotheses, accelerate translational research or reduce the cost of experimentation. Future evaluations therefore need to include prospective assessments embedded within real research programmes, on subjects such as target prioritization and experimental testing. These evaluations should also consider practical measures of utility, such as token cost or time-to-completion, relative to manual human research.
A further frontier lies in multimodal scientific reasoning. The current implementation focuses primarily on literature and structured biomedical databases. However, much of modern biomedical research depends equally on imaging, single-cell transcriptomics, spatial biology, structural biology, pathology, proteomics and increasingly complex experimental datasets. Integrating these diverse modalities into coherent evidence representations represents an important opportunity for future research. Similarly, closer integration with laboratory automation and ingestion of experimental data could enable evidence-centric agents to not only interpret existing knowledge but also propose, execute and iteratively refine new experiments.
Perhaps the most interesting question raised by this work is not whether evidence graphs represent the optimal implementation, but whether scientific AI itself should be viewed less as a sophisticated chatbot and more as a computational research collaborator or a thought-partner. Human scientists spend relatively little time recalling isolated facts. Instead, they continually organize, challenge and refine evidence into evolving conceptual models. If AI systems are to participate meaningfully in scientific discovery, they may require analogous capabilities.
DeepEvidence therefore represents more than another biomedical agent. It illustrates a broader conceptual transition in scientific AI, from systems that retrieve information, towards systems that organize evidence in support of scientific reasoning. Whether evidence-centric architectures ultimately become the dominant paradigm with deep adoption within the biomedical domain remains to be seen. However, the work by Wang et al.1 suggests that the future of scientific AI may depend less on generating convincing answers than on constructing trustworthy representations of the evidence from which those answers arise.

items.title: Emotional optimization by newsroom AI needs behavioural evaluation
items.summary:
Nature Machine Intelligence, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s42256-026-01315-8

When newsroom artificial intelligence (AI) engages in emotional packaging, it changes how a story feels, shaping whether people approach, trust and share it. As these systems are designed and deployed, AI and behavioural researchers should work together to test whether emotional packaging helps accurate information reach readers, and whether it deepens division.
